narrative:
The model estimates you have a 12% chance of failing your final year, which is low but enough for the school to require you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The prediction that you will fail is driven mainly by three factors, ranked by importance. First, your reason for choosing this school—reputation—pushed the model toward predicting failure. Most students who passed chose the school for its course offerings rather than its reputation, so this choice worked against you. Second, having zero past class failures actually pulled the prediction slightly toward passing, which is typical since students who passed also had no prior failures on average. Third, your strong desire to pursue higher education also nudged the outcome toward passing, as every student who ultimately passed shared this same ambition.

Even though two of the top factors leaned positive, the negative influence from your school-choice motivation was strong enough to tip the overall prediction into the failure zone, triggering the obligation for extra courses.

To improve, consider focusing more on your actual coursework and study habits rather than the school's reputation. Since you already want to continue studying after school and have no history of failing classes, building consistent daily study routines and reducing your very high level of going out with friends could help turn that 12% risk into a clear pass.
